paragraphs: This CB Radio gives a truck cab or a dispatch desk the boxy transceiver that long-haul drivers keep bolted under the dashboard. The mesh runs to 51,222 polygons and 52,306 vertices, most of them spent on the knobs, the channel display and the vented casing. A coiled cord leads to a handheld microphone, the detail that makes the unit read instantly in a close shot.

Its unwrap is non-overlapping, so a painter can bake wear onto the faceplate without fighting stacked islands. The build carries CheckMate Lite certification, which confirms clean geometry and a sensible file structure on import. Rubbed paint around the volume dial is easy to add, since each control sits on its own clear patch of the map.

Buyers pick between two versions at $69 each, a plain unbranded unit and a Cobra variant with its familiar front panel. On sale from 2020, the radio fits trucking films, roadside diner scenes and retro electronics renders. Game artists drop it into cab interiors where a glowing channel number adds life to an otherwise static dashboard.

Compact Assault Rifle suits close-quarters scenes where a short barrel, a folding stock and a curved magazine must read clearly in a hand. Most of the 83,910 polygons go into the receiver, the cocking handle and the ribbed handguard, so the silhouette holds at close range. The 44,603 vertices point to a triangulated, game-friendly cage rather than a dense subdivision mesh.

Unwrapping stays non-overlapping across the whole weapon, which leaves room to bake scratches where a gloved hand would wear the finish. CheckMate Pro certification on this gun means its topology, naming and scale passed the strictest inspection TurboSquid runs. Sights and sling mounts are separated cleanly enough to accept their own material without any extra cutting.

The page offers two versions, the main rifle at $69 and an MP5 Semi Automatic at $39 for tighter budgets. Released in 2023, the weapon goes into tactical shooters, police procedural footage and training material on firearm handling. A SWAT officer carrying it through a narrow corridor is exactly the kind of shot it was built to serve.

Covered Cadaver puts a draped body on a steel morgue tray, the quiet centerpiece of an autopsy room or a crime drama. The 133,460 polygons go mostly into the sheet, whose folds settle over the head, shoulders and feet in a believable way. With 67,222 vertices the mesh is triangulated, which keeps the cloth shape locked and stable in any renderer.

Its UV islands never overlap, so a stain or a toe tag can be painted onto the fabric without repeating. The asset holds CheckMate Pro certification, the top TurboSquid grade for clean topology and consistent scale. Polished metal on the tray contrasts with the matte sheet, and the two surfaces take separate shaders without fuss.

A pair of versions costs $69 apiece, the plain tray and a CSI Jevett gurney variant on a mobile cart. Out since 2023, the scene piece works for forensic series, medical training on postmortem procedure and horror game levels. Placed under a cold overhead lamp, the shrouded form tells the story of the room before any character speaks.

Dance Studio Interior gives you a complete rehearsal room with a wooden floor, a mirrored wall and a barre for ballet scenes. The hall is modeled at real-world scale, so dancers and cameras fit inside without a rescaling pass before the shoot. The 401,181 polygons and 403,552 vertices cover window frames, ceiling fixtures and the long handrail running along the mirrors.

Every surface is unwrapped without overlap, letting you bake daylight from the tall windows straight onto the floorboards. The room is built to CheckMate specification, which keeps its topology clean and its objects grouped in a sensible order. Reflections in the mirror wall double the space visually, a handy trick for a wide establishing frame.

There are two versions at $69 each, this classic room and a Professional Ballet Studio with Mirrors. Introduced in 2025, the interior suits architectural walkthroughs, music videos and character animation of a dance lesson. A single figure stretching at the barre is enough to turn the empty hall into a finished picture.

Disposable Protective Clothing gives a lab, a factory floor or a quarantine scene the white hooded coverall a worker steps into. At 126.78 x 39.9 x H188.44 cm, the suit matches an adult figure and keeps its sleeves held away from the body. The 37,830 polygons trace the zipper, the elastic cuffs and the loose creases that thin fabric forms at the knees.

UV mapping is mixed, so some parts share texture space while others get islands of their own. The garment conforms to CheckMate specification, meaning tidy topology and a scale that holds on import. Its 39,519 vertices give enough density for a cloth simulation pass if the coverall needs to move.

You get two versions priced at $69, this coverall and a Full-Body Disposable Suit with Hood and Gloves. A 2025 release, it suits pandemic footage, cleanroom visualization and safety training for chemical or industrial sites. Hung on a hook beside a decontamination door, the empty outfit also works as quiet set dressing.

Food Containers Collection fills a kitchen shelf, a deli counter or a packaging render with an assortment of tubs, trays and lidded boxes. Grouping the pieces in one purchase saves hunting for matching packaging across separate files and keeps the style consistent. Each container has a clean, simple shape, so it reads at once on a pantry shelf or inside an open fridge.

The set carries CheckMate Pro certification, the strictest TurboSquid check for topology, naming and scale. Simple forms like these suit label work, since a flat side takes a printed sticker without stretching the artwork. Translucent plastic is the usual look here, and a glossy shader with a light tint sells it quickly.

Two versions are on offer, this first set at $69 and a second Food Containers 3D Models Collection 2 at $39. Available since 2016, the bundle belongs to the older core of the catalog and still turns up in product shots. Meal delivery apps, grocery store scenes and food storage tutorials are typical homes for these little boxes.

Gaming VR Headset shows a woman wearing a coral virtual reality visor, ready for immersive tech scenes and simulator promos without extra posing. The figure and device total 47,923 polygons and 58,303 vertices, with the strap, face cushion and sensor panel modeled as real parts. At 26.95 x 29.22 x H36.5 cm, the head and headset sit at true scale for close portraits.

Its UVs overlap, so some mirrored pieces share texture space, which keeps the maps compact but limits unique painting. The model follows CheckMate specification, giving clean topology and sensible object names when it opens in a new scene. Blonde hair frames the visor, and the contrast between soft strands and hard plastic reads well under studio light.

Shoppers choose between two versions, this one and a Gaming VR Headset with Dual Strap on Head, both priced at $69. Launched in 2025, it serves game trailers, medical simulation interfaces and articles on virtual reality hardware. A soft rim light along the visor edge is all it takes to make the device glow in a dark frame.

Hand Wearing Whoop 4 Tracker White places a slim fitness band on a relaxed wrist, ideal for wearable tech close-ups and health app scenes. The mesh holds 30,572 polygons over 15,630 vertices, a triangulated build that keeps the knuckles, nails and strap clasp crisp. Because the band has no screen, the knit strap and the sensor pod carry the whole look of the device.

UV layout is non-overlapping, so skin pores and the fabric weave of the strap can each get unique detail. The asset passed CheckMate Pro inspection, which confirms quad discipline, correct scale and tidy naming. Pale strap material sits against warm skin tones, and that contrast helps the tracker stand out in a crop.

The page bundles two versions at $69, this white edition and an Activity Tracker Whoop 4 Blue on Hand Blue. Published in 2023, the hand suits sports science explainers, product renders for fitness startups and training app onboarding screens. Framed against a gym bench or a running track, the wrist becomes a convincing still for a health story.

Hoversurf S3 Compact Aircraft models a single-seat electric hoverbike, the kind of personal flying machine that shows up in near-future city scenes. Its 203,468 polygons and 105,141 vertices go into ducted rotors, a sculpted seat and the handlebar controls between them. Exposed propellers inside each duct give the craft its distinctive look and invite a spinning animation pass.

The unwrap is non-overlapping, so carbon fiber patterns and warning decals can be laid out without collisions. StemCell certification means the file opens consistently across major renderers with matching materials and scale. Bright body panels contrast with dark rotor housings, and that split makes the silhouette easy to read from below.

Two versions sit on the page at $69 each, this branded craft and a generic Compact Aircraft without the maker name. On the market since 2023, the drone bike fits mobility concept films, sci-fi games and pieces on urban air transport. Hovering above a rooftop at dusk, the machine sells the idea of tomorrow's commute in a single image.

Man Hand Middle Finger Sign captures the rude gesture in a clean, posed male hand, handy for comedy scenes, memes and character close-ups. With only 6,512 polygons and 3,268 vertices, the hand stays light enough to attach to a figure or repeat across a crowd. Folded fingers press into the palm while the raised digit stands straight, so the gesture reads at any distance.

Its UVs are laid out without overlap, giving room to paint wrinkles over the knuckles and a realistic nail bed. The mesh holds CheckMate Pro certification, so topology and scale already meet the top TurboSquid standard. Skin tone is easy to shift with a single shader, which helps match the hand to any character it joins.

The page lists two versions, this gesture at $69 and a Man Hand OK Pose at $39 for a friendlier sign. Made available in 2024, the hand serves animated shorts, social media clips and game cutscenes where an insult needs no words. Shot against a plain backdrop, the pose works as a bold graphic element for a poster or a sticker.

16 Inch Telescope with Tripod recreates a large observatory-grade instrument on a fork mount, perfect for backyard astronomy and planetarium scenes. The 75,954 polygons cover the wide tube, the fork arms, the drive base and the heavy tripod legs. A finder scope and an eyepiece holder sit on the tube, small details that sell the instrument up close.

UV islands do not overlap, so scratches on the black tube and labels on the base can be painted with unique detail. CheckMate Pro certification confirms clean topology over the 78,172 vertices and a scale that behaves on import. The broad aperture faces the sky in a way a camera can frame from low angles for drama.

Two versions appear at $69 each, this model and a Telescope 16 Inch with Tripod that mirrors it under another title. Released in 2021, the scope fits science education, hobby store renders and night-sky films about amateur stargazers. Placed on a dark lawn under a star field, the instrument immediately sets the mood of a quiet observing night.

8 Inch Telescope with Tripod offers a compact fork-mounted scope for hobby astronomers, sized for a balcony, a campsite or a classroom. Its 68,969 polygons and 71,162 vertices define the short tube, the hand controller cable and the folding field tripod. The fork cradles the tube from both sides, a recognizable shape that tells viewers this is a serious amateur tool.

The unwrap stays free of overlap, which lets you add dust on the dew shield and worn labels near the focus knob. This build passed CheckMate Pro inspection, so its topology and naming meet the top TurboSquid bar. Matte black parts sit against a lighter tube finish, giving lighting artists clear separation for rim highlights.

There are two versions at $69, this one and a Telescope 8 Inch with Tripod sharing the same geometry under a different name. Introduced in 2021, the scope suits educational animations, outdoor gear catalogs and short films about a first night under the stars. Pair it with a red flashlight and a folding chair for a believable field observing setup.

Military Transport Aircraft Scale Model with Stand shows a heavy airlifter as a desktop collectible, mounted on a display pedestal. The 15,847 polygons and 16,467 vertices keep the high wing, the T-tail and the engine pods light and readable. Because it is a model kit rather than a full aircraft, it belongs on an office desk or a museum shelf.

UVs are non-overlapping, so tail markings and a grey camouflage can be painted at full resolution across the airframe. CheckMate Pro certification guarantees the topology, scale and file layout pass the strictest TurboSquid checks. A slim metal rod lifts the plane off its base, letting light pass underneath for an elegant studio shot.

Buyers can choose either of two versions, the generic airlifter or a Globemaster III Scale Model with Stand, each costing $69. On sale since 2021, the piece suits office interiors, military museum scenes and aviation gift renders. Set beside a framed photo and a coffee mug, the replica gives a commander's desk an instant sense of rank.

Milk Bottles Collection brings a row of glass and plastic dairy bottles to a breakfast table, a farm shop or a fridge shelf scene. Having the shapes in one bundle keeps caps, labels and proportions consistent across a whole kitchen layout. Wide shoulders and narrow necks on the bottles make the silhouettes familiar even in a quick background pass.

The pack meets CheckMate specification, so every piece arrives with clean topology and the same sense of scale. White liquid behind clear glass needs only a simple layered shader, and the thick bottle walls help refraction look right. Flat label bands around the middle accept branding art without distortion, which suits packaging comps.

Two versions are offered, this first set at $69 and a Milk Bottles Collection 2 at $49 with other shapes. New in 2026, the bundle fits grocery visualization, dairy farm animations and food styling mockups. Lined up on a windowsill with morning light behind them, the bottles create a calm still life almost by themselves.

Mining Locomotive on Railway Section shows a rusted underground loco on a short stretch of narrow-gauge track, built for tunnel and quarry scenes. The 82,931 polygons and 82,821 vertices cover the cab, the battery box, the couplers and the wheel sets resting on the rails. Peeling paint and corroded panels make it read as a machine that hauled ore for decades.

There are 11 texture maps at 4096 x 4096, enough resolution for close shots of rust streaks and flaking enamel. UVs never overlap, so each patch of grime is unique rather than tiled from one area. StemCell certification means the materials behave consistently across the main renderers without manual rewiring.

The page holds two versions with the same title at $69 each, giving a choice of file setup for different pipelines. Around since 2020, the loco fits abandoned mine environments, industrial history documentaries and survival game levels. A single headlamp beam cutting through tunnel dust is all the scene needs to feel cold and deep underground.

Gantry with Hoist provides a portable steel frame with a chain hoist, the workhorse of garages, workshops and small factory bays. It stands at 335.35 x 203.38 x H280.9 cm, close to the size of a real shop crane on caster wheels. The 154,600 polygons describe the I-beam, the A-frame legs, the trolley and the hanging hook block.

UV mapping is mixed, combining shared and unique islands, so repeated bolts reuse texture space efficiently. StemCell certification ensures the materials translate cleanly between renderers, which saves setup time in mixed pipelines. With 152,667 vertices the frame keeps sharp bevels on its welded joints, and those edges catch light nicely.

Two versions come at $69 each, this one and an Adjustable Steel Gantry with Powered Chain Hoist Blue. A 2025 addition, the crane serves workshop interiors, engine lifting animations and safety training on overhead loads. Hang an engine block from the hook and the frame instantly explains what it is for.

Oil Refinery Control Station Building gives a petrochemical plant its operations hub, a blocky structure with pipes, ladders and service doors. The 102,802 polygons and 110,291 vertices go into the walls, rooftop units, handrails and the cabling that links the building to the site. Industrial cladding and external stairs make it fit naturally beside tanks and distillation columns.

Its UVs overlap, which means some repeated panels share texture space and keep the maps economical. StemCell certification supports consistent material behavior across major renderers, which matters when the station joins a large plant scene. Strong vertical lines on the facade give the camera a clear rhythm from a drone fly-over angle.

For $69 apiece there are two versions, this structure or an Operations Station Red with a bolder color scheme. Released in 2024, the building suits energy sector visualization, industrial game maps and safety briefing animations. Surrounded by pipe racks and floodlights at night, the station becomes the obvious focal point of a refinery shot.

Padded Cell Interior builds a soft-walled isolation room, the classic setting for psychiatric dramas, thrillers and horror sequences. The room spans 657.6 x 666.16 x H504.25 cm, giving a camera crew space to circle a character inside. Quilted panels cover every wall, and their repeated tufts create the oppressive pattern the setting is known for.

UVs are non-overlapping, so stains, scuffs and tears can be painted onto the padding without visible repeats. Built to CheckMate specification, the 141,099 polygons follow clean topology that subdivides predictably. The 143,860 vertices keep the puffed cushions rounded, which matters when light rakes across them from a single fixture.

Two versions can be bought, the cell itself or a Mental Hospital Padded Room, and either one costs $69. Out from 2025, the interior serves film previsualization, escape room game levels and asylum horror trailers. A lone figure in a straitjacket under a flickering ceiling lamp turns the empty room into a frightening frame.

Pholcus Phalangioides recreates the cellar spider, a tiny body hung on long, thread-thin legs that cast spindly shadows on a wall. The model uses 27,708 polygons over 13,968 vertices, enough for the jointed legs, the oval abdomen and the small cephalothorax. Leg segments bend at natural angles, so the creature looks as if it is resting in its web.

The UV layout has no overlap, letting you paint banding on the legs and translucent patches on the abdomen. StemCell certification keeps shading consistent across renderers, which helps macro shots match between tools. Its pale, semi-transparent body responds beautifully to subsurface scattering under a side light.

Two versions sit at $69 each, this spider and a Pholcidae Fur variant with fine hair for close macro work. Available since 2024, it suits nature documentaries, entomology lessons and creepy corners of a horror game. Dangling from a dusty ceiling beam, the spider adds instant atmosphere to any abandoned house interior.

Photography Light Collection equips a virtual studio with softboxes, stands and reflectors for behind-the-scenes renders and set planning. Having the gear in one pack keeps stand heights, clamps and cable details consistent across a whole shoot layout. Folding legs and tall telescoping poles give each fixture the recognizable look of a working photo kit.

The set holds CheckMate Pro certification, confirming clean topology, correct scale and logical naming on every item. Diffuser fabric and metal hardware take separate materials, so a glowing panel can sit on a matte black stand. Lights can double as real emitters in a scene, turning the props into practical sources for the frame.

There are two versions, this kit at $69 and a Photography Light Collection 2 at $89 with additional fixtures. Released in 2022, the collection serves studio interior visualization, filmmaking tutorials and product shoot planning. Arranged around an empty stool, the lights tell viewers a portrait session is about to begin.

Photography Studio Interior lays out a ready shooting space with a cyclorama backdrop, light stands and a working floor plan for set renders. The 218,217 polygons and 223,594 vertices cover the curved backdrop, fixtures, cables and furniture around the edges. The seamless cyc wall removes the floor line, which is exactly what a product or portrait shot needs.

UVs are non-overlapping across the scene, so footprints and tape marks on the floor can be painted uniquely. Conforming to CheckMate specification, the room keeps clean topology and sensible object groups for quick edits. Dark walls around the bright backdrop help control bounce light and give the space a professional mood.

Two variants are sold for $69 apiece, this room and a Black Interior Photo Studio Black for darker sets. A 2024 piece, the interior suits photography courses, fashion shoot previsualization and creative agency scenes. Drop in a model on a stool and a camera on a tripod, and the frame is complete.

Pinatas Collection brings colorful paper party figures to birthday scenes, fiesta decor and festive product shots in one ready group. Each figure carries the layered paper fringe that gives a pinata its fluffy, ruffled outline. Bright, saturated colors make the set a cheerful anchor for any celebration render.

The bundle passed CheckMate Pro inspection, so every shape meets the top TurboSquid standard for topology and scale. Fringe strips catch rim light along their edges, and a slight sheen on the paper adds depth without fuss. Hanging loops at the top make it easy to suspend the figures from a rope or a tree branch.

Two versions are available: the original pack costs $69, while a Pinatas Collection 2 with a wider range runs $129. Around since 2017, the bundle suits party planning apps, children's animation and Mexican fiesta scenes. Hung above a table of sweets with paper streamers, the figures turn a plain backyard into a celebration.

Stents with Artery shows mesh tubes placed inside a cut-open blood vessel, a clear teaching aid for cardiology and vascular surgery. The 20,640 polygons and 20,328 vertices define the lattice of the stents and the curved wall of the artery around them. The open section reveals how the metal scaffold presses against the vessel lining.

UVs are non-overlapping, so vessel tissue and metal lattice can each get their own detailed textures. Made to CheckMate specification, the model keeps clean geometry suited to medical animation and close inspection. Translucent artery walls let viewers see the implant inside, which a soft backlight makes even clearer.

You will find two versions under one title at $69 each, so you can choose the file setup that fits your pipeline. Out since 2024, the piece fits patient education, medical device explainers and hospital training videos. Rotating slowly on a white background, the cutaway gives a clear picture of the procedure in seconds.

Pressure Washer models a portable electric cleaner with a hose reel, a spray wand and a wheeled body for patio and car scenes. At 35.67 x 39.72 x H54.77 cm, the unit fits naturally beside a person, a garden path or a parked vehicle. The 113,072 polygons describe the handle, the cable hook, the nozzle and the vented motor housing.

UVs overlap in places, so mirrored parts share texture space, which keeps the material set compact. StemCell certification ensures the gray plastic and black rubber look the same across major renderers. With 121,141 vertices the rounded housing stays smooth, and its soft curves pick up a clean specular sweep.

Two versions are available at $69, this gray unit and a Ryobi Electric Pressure Washer 2000 PSI Green. Introduced in 2025, the cleaner suits home improvement content, garden tool renders and car detailing animations. Show it next to a wet driveway with a fine mist from the nozzle, and the scene explains itself.

Production Center gives an industrial site a long factory hall with loading gates and a front office block, sized for city and plant scenes. Everything sits at true scale, so trucks and workers sit at true scale around it. With just 20,651 polygons the building stays light enough to repeat across a large industrial district.

UVs are non-overlapping, letting you paint dirt runs and company signage across the facade without repeats. Following CheckMate specification, the structure keeps tidy topology over its 24,665 vertices and simple grouping. Ribbed wall panels and a low pitched roof match the look of modern prefabricated plants.

Two versions cost $69 each here, this hall and a Production Center UralSpetsTrans tied to a real manufacturer. A 2025 release, the building fits urban planning renders, logistics games and corporate presentations about manufacturing. Add a few semi trailers at the docks and the site immediately reads as a working facility.
